title: Across the Moor
paragraphs: She slept for a long time. When she woke, Mrs. Medlock had bought a lunch basket at one of the stations, and they ate some chicken, cold beef, bread and butter, and drank hot tea. The rain seemed to be pouring down harder than ever, and everyone in the station wore wet, shining waterproof coats. The guard lit the lamps in the carriage, and Mrs. Medlock grew very cheerful over her tea, chicken and beef. She ate a great deal and then fell asleep herself. Mary sat and stared at her, watching her fine bonnet slide to one side, until she dozed off again in her own corner of the carriage, lulled by the rain splashing against the windows. It was quite dark when she woke the next time. The train had stopped at a station, and Mrs. Medlock was shaking her.
“You’ve had a good sleep!” she said. “Time to open your eyes! We’re at Thwaite Station, and we’ve got a long drive ahead of us.”

Mary stood up and tried to keep her eyes open while Mrs. Medlock gathered her parcels. The little girl did not offer to help. In India, native servants always picked things up and carried them, and it seemed perfectly proper to her that other people should wait on you.

The station was small, and nobody but the two of them seemed to be getting off the train. The station-master spoke to Mrs. Medlock in a rough, friendly way. He pronounced his words in a strange, broad manner that Mary later learned was Yorkshire.
“I see you’ve got back,” he said. “And you’ve brought the young one with you.”
“Aye, that’s her,” answered Mrs. Medlock. She spoke with a Yorkshire accent herself, and she jerked her head back over her shoulder toward Mary. “How’s your Missus?”
“Well enough. The carriage is waiting outside for you.”

A brougham stood on the road in front of the little open platform. Mary saw that it was a smart carriage, and that the footman who helped her in was smart too. His long waterproof coat and the waterproof cover on his hat were shining and dripping with rain, just like everything else, including the burly station-master.

The footman shut the door and climbed up beside the coachman, and they drove off. The little girl found herself in a comfortably cushioned corner, but she did not feel like going back to sleep. She sat looking out of the window. She was curious to see something of the road that was taking her to the strange place Mrs. Medlock had talked about. She was not a timid child at all, and she was not exactly frightened. But she felt that anything might happen in a house with a hundred rooms, nearly all of them shut up—a house standing at the edge of a moor.
“What is a moor?” she asked Mrs. Medlock suddenly.

“Look out of the window in about ten minutes and you’ll see,” the woman answered. “We have to drive five miles across Missel Moor before we reach the Manor. You won’t see much, because it’s a dark night, but you’ll see something.”

Mary asked no more questions. She waited in the darkness of her corner, keeping her eyes on the window. The carriage lamps threw light a little way ahead, and she caught glimpses of the things they passed. After leaving the station, they had driven through a tiny village, and she had seen whitewashed cottages and the lights of a public house. Then they had passed a church and a vicarage. In one cottage there was a little shop window with toys, sweets and odd things set out for sale. Then they were on the highroad, and she saw hedges and trees. After that there seemed to be nothing different for a long time—or at least it felt like a long time to her.

At last the horses began to slow down, as if they were climbing uphill. Soon there seemed to be no more hedges and no more trees. In fact, she could see nothing but thick darkness on either side. She leaned forward and pressed her face against the window just as the carriage gave a big jolt.
“Eh! We’re on the moor now, sure enough,” said Mrs. Medlock.

The carriage lamps cast a yellow light on a rough road that seemed to be cut through bushes and low, scrubby plants. Beyond them lay the great dark expanse that spread out in front of them and all around. A wind was rising, and it made a strange, wild, low, rushing sound.
“It’s—it’s not the sea, is it?” said Mary, looking around at her companion.

“No, not at all,” answered Mrs. Medlock. “It isn’t fields or mountains either. It’s just miles and miles and miles of wild land where nothing grows but heather and gorse and broom, and nothing lives but wild ponies and sheep.”
“I feel as if it might be the sea, if there were water on it,” said Mary. “It sounds like the sea right now.”
“That’s the wind blowing through the bushes,” Mrs. Medlock said. “It’s a wild, dreary sort of place, if you ask me, though plenty of people like it—especially when the heather’s in bloom.”

On and on they drove through the darkness. The rain stopped, but the wind rushed past and whistled and made strange sounds. The road went up and down, and several times the carriage crossed a little bridge, with water rushing very fast and noisily underneath. Mary felt as if the drive would never end. The wide, bleak moor seemed to her like a vast black ocean, and she was crossing it on a narrow strip of dry land.
“I don’t like it,” she said to herself. “I don’t like it,” and she pressed her thin lips more tightly together.
The horses were climbing a hilly stretch of road when she first caught sight of a light. Mrs. Medlock saw it just as soon as she did, and she let out a long sigh of relief.
“Eh, I’m glad to see that bit of light twinkling,” she exclaimed. “It’s the light in the lodge window. We’ll get a good cup of tea before long, at any rate.”

It was “before long,” as she had said, but not very soon. When the carriage passed through the park gates, there were still two miles of avenue to drive through. The trees nearly met overhead, so it felt as if they were driving through a long, dark tunnel.

They drove out of the tunnel into an open space and stopped in front of an immensely long but low house that seemed to ramble around a stone courtyard. At first Mary thought there were no lights at all in the windows. But as she got out of the carriage, she saw that one room in a corner upstairs showed a dull glow.

The front door was huge, made of massive, oddly shaped panels of oak, studded with big iron nails and bound with great iron bars. It opened into an enormous hall, so dimly lit that the faces in the portraits on the walls and the figures in the suits of armor made Mary not want to look at them. As she stood on the stone floor, she looked like a very small, odd little black figure, and she felt as small and lost and odd as she looked.
A neat, thin old man stood near the manservant who opened the door for them.
“You are to take her to her room,” he said in a husky voice. “He doesn’t want to see her. He’s going to London in the morning.”
“Very well, Mr. Pitcher,” Mrs. Medlock answered. “As long as I know what’s expected of me, I can manage.”
“What’s expected of you, Mrs. Medlock,” Mr. Pitcher said, “is that you make sure he isn’t disturbed, and that he doesn’t see what he doesn’t want to see.”

Then Mary Lennox was led up a broad staircase, down a long corridor, up a short flight of steps, and through one corridor after another. At last a door opened in a wall, and she found herself in a room with a fire burning and a supper laid out on a table.
Mrs. Medlock said bluntly:
“Well, here you are! This room and the next one are where you’ll live—and you must stay in them. Don’t you forget that!”
That was how Mistress Mary arrived at Misselthwaite Manor, and she had perhaps never felt so contrary in all her life.
